How to paste one of these

  1. Canvas Calendar, click the day, Edit, then More Options.
  2. Title the event exactly as given on the topic below.
  3. In the Rich Content Editor, click the </> icon to open the HTML editor. Never paste into the visual editor. Pasting rendered HTML there injects wrapper <div>s and inline font declarations that collapse the table.
  4. Press Copy the HTML below, then paste into that HTML editor.
  5. Switch back to the visual editor, delete the [INSERT ASSIGNMENT LINK] placeholder, and insert the real assignment from the right-hand course-links panel, Assignments, click the assignment. Do not hand-type that link; see Section 5 of CANVAS-BUILD-GUIDE.md for why.
  6. Save.

Topic 1

CE - SM1 - Where the Money Comes From

Follow the money backwards, one step at a time

Event title
CE - SM1 - Where the Money Comes From
Assignment to link
none, this topic is done on paper
What it will look like in Canvas

OVERVIEW

Every app you opened today was free, and not one of those companies is a charity. Today you build the chain backwards: from you opening an app to somebody getting paid, one box and one arrow at a time. You will do it on paper, because a device turns a trace into copy-paste from a search result. Then you walk the room and read four other chains, which is where you find out what you left out.

LEARNING TARGETS
  1. I can trace the chain that connects me opening a free app to a company getting paid.
  2. I can explain what a company gets from me when I pay it no money at all.
  3. I can compare my chain with other people's and say where they agree and where they do not.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  1. I can draw a chain with at least four boxes in it and no gap I cannot explain out loud.
  2. I can name the thing being sold, who is buying it, and who is being sold.
  3. I can name one box I got wrong or left out after reading four other chains, and say which chain changed my mind.

Topic 2

CE - SM2 - Somebody Made a Film About This

Your job is not to agree with it

Event title
CE - SM2 - Somebody Made a Film About This
Assignment to link
none, this topic is done on paper

Do not name the film anywhere in Canvas before this topic runs. The event title, the module header and the assignment name all stay vague on purpose. A student who looks the title up in advance reads what they are supposed to conclude and arrives having concluded it.

What it will look like in Canvas

OVERVIEW

Somebody made a film about the thing you traced last class. We are going to watch it. Your job is not to agree with it, and it is not to disagree with it either. Your job is to do to the film exactly what you did to your app: take it apart, find out how it works, and see where the money is. Every film was made by somebody, for a reason, with money from somewhere.

LEARNING TARGETS
  1. I can identify who made this film, who speaks in it, and what each of them has to gain.
  2. I can name a persuasion technique the film uses and explain how it works on a viewer.
  3. I can separate what the film proves from what it only suggests.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  1. I can say who made the film and point to one thing in it that tells me what it wants me to believe.
  2. I can point at one specific scene and name the technique it uses on me.
  3. I can state one claim the film makes that I would want to check, and say what evidence would settle it.

Topic 3

CE - SM3 - Inside the Algorithm Box

What the app counts, and what it does with the count

Event title
CE - SM3 - Inside the Algorithm Box
Assignment to link
SM3 - Inside the Algorithm · 20 points
What it will look like in Canvas

OVERVIEW

Almost every chain in the room had a box in the middle where the app watches what you do. Nobody wrote what was inside it, because none of us knew. Today you open it. You will find out what an app counts about you when you are not posting, what it does with the count, and why two people who open the same app at the same second see different things.

LEARNING TARGETS
  1. I can name what an app counts about me when I have not posted, liked, or commented on anything.
  2. I can explain the feedback loop that makes an app better at holding my attention the longer I use it.
  3. I can explain that a ranking system pushes on a number a person chose, and predict what that choice costs.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  1. I can list three engagement signals an app collects without me sending it anything.
  2. I can explain, out loud, why two people who open the same app at the same second see different things.
  3. I can name a number an app could optimize for, and say what would go wrong with that choice.

Topic 4

CE - SM4 - What It Does to You, and What It Keeps

Evidence about effects, and a record that does not delete

Event title
CE - SM4 - What It Does to You, and What It Keeps
Assignment to link
SM4 - Effects and Your Footprint · 20 points
What it will look like in Canvas

OVERVIEW

Two questions today, and they are different kinds of question. First: what does social media do to how you feel? That one has real research behind it, the research disagrees with itself, and your job is to learn to read a disagreement rather than pick a side. Second: what does the app keep after you close it? That one is not a debate. It is a record, it is longer than what you posted, and people who make decisions about your future can read part of it.

LEARNING TARGETS
  1. I can name a positive and a negative effect of social media, and say what would have to be true for either one to be a cause rather than a coincidence.
  2. I can explain why two honest researchers looking at the same teenagers reach opposite conclusions about harm.
  3. I can describe what my digital footprint contains, and name one decision somebody could make about me from it.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  1. I can state a claim about social media and mental health, and say whether the evidence behind it shows a cause or only a pattern.
  2. I can name two things I would want to know about a study before I believed its headline.
  3. I can name three places a piece of my footprint sits that I cannot delete myself.

Topic 5

CE - SM5 - How a Lie Travels

Fake news, the tactics that carry it, and elections

Event title
CE - SM5 - How a Lie Travels
Assignment to link
SM5 - How a Lie Travels · 20 points
What it will look like in Canvas

OVERVIEW

Today is the part of this unit everybody thinks they are already good at. You will find out that spotting false information is mostly not about the false information. It is about what carries it: emotion, headlines built to be clicked, accounts that are not people, and a ranking system that rewards whatever gets a reaction. Then you will learn the actual checking, which takes about ninety seconds, and find out what the research says about who does the spreading. The answer to that last one is not what most people assume.

LEARNING TARGETS
  1. I can name four tactics that make false information spread, and explain what each one does to the reader.
  2. I can check an unfamiliar claim in under two minutes, and say specifically what I checked.
  3. I can explain one specific mechanism by which false information affects an election, beyond people believing wrong things.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  1. I can name the feeling a piece of content is aiming for, and say why that feeling helps it spread.
  2. I can trace a claim back to its earliest source, or say honestly that I looked and could not find one.
  3. I can explain the difference between a claim that is false and a claim that is true but framed to mislead.

Topic 6

CE - SM6 - Who Gets to Decide?

You, the company, or the government

Event title
CE - SM6 - Who Gets to Decide?
Assignment to link
SM6 - Who Decides · 20 points
What it will look like in Canvas

OVERVIEW

On the first day I told you I would ask you a hard question at the end, and this is it: who should get to decide what a platform is allowed to do to your attention, you, the company, or the government? You traced the money, took a film apart, opened the algorithm box, weighed the research on what it does to people, and followed a false story through the system, so today is a real argument instead of opinions. You will not be graded on which side you land.

LEARNING TARGETS
  1. I can state all three answers to who should decide, and give the strongest case and the hardest question for each one.
  2. I can name the tradeoff in a position, including the one I hold, because an answer with no tradeoff in it is not finished.
  3. I can use an earlier fight over a new medium as a precedent, by naming what is the same and what is different.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  1. I can state the position I did not pick well enough that somebody who holds it would say I got it right.
  2. I can answer the hardest question against my own position, rather than restating why I am right.
  3. I can name what would change my mind, specifically enough that somebody could go looking for it.
